unit.title: Mark off/out structural fabrications and shapes

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan, lead and check the marking out of structural steelwork and fabricated shapes. You will check beams, columns, channels and angles before marking, mark hole groups, copes, notches, stiffeners and weld preparations, set out trusses, frames and stair stringers full size, and allow for weld shrinkage, camber, bending and rolling. You will also develop patterns for cones, transitions and pipe intersections, and keep the checks and records that make structural work fit on site.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers marking out on **structural sections** (beams, columns, channels, angles and hollow sections), **full-size setting out** of trusses, frames and stairs, and **developments**: the flat patterns for cones, hoppers, transitions and pipe intersections. The general marking-out skills (datums, tools, punching, templates) are covered in Mark off/out (general engineering), MEMCOR0081B; this unit builds on them.

Structural work is large and heavy, and it must fit parts made by other people: columns on bolts already cast in concrete, beams onto cleats on site, a roof onto walls. A few millimetres wrong at the marking stage can mean a beam that will not bolt up 6 m in the air. At Level 3 you plan the marking, do the geometry, lead the team, check every piece and keep the records.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and fabricators, platers and team leaders in structural and plate shops.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Handle heavy sections safely
Plan lifts and turns, use cranes, stands and trestles within their safe working load, and never work under a suspended load.
Read structural drawings
Work from the shop drawing for each piece mark; find the datums; raise queries on clashes and errors.
Check the steel
Check section size, length, sweep, camber, twist and damage before marking; measure long lengths accurately.
Mark members
Mark hole groups on gauge lines and back marks, with the right pitch, end and edge distances; mark skew cuts and piece marks.
Mark copes, notches, stiffeners and preparations
Size and mark copes with a radius, notches for bending, stiffeners with snipes, and bevel lines to the WPS.
Set out full size
Set out trusses, frames and stair stringers on the floor or plate table, check them, and use them to mark members and gussets.
Allow for shrinkage, camber, bending and rolling
Work out and mark the allowances so the finished part is the right size and shape.
Develop patterns
Find true lengths and develop patterns by parallel line, radial line and triangulation, including pipe branches and lobster-back bends.
Check, record and lead
First-off and second-person checks, check sheets, piece marks, records, and a team that knows its jobs.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on drawings, datums, structural sections, measuring, checking members, copes and notches, stiffeners, trusses, calculations, allowances, developments, pipe intersections, templates, hole marking, tolerances, site fit, safety, tools, quality checks and team leading.
A **written paper** with short answers (names and calculated sizes) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two team practicals**: setting out a small roof truss full size, marking the members and gussets from it and recording the checks; and developing a square-to-round transition by triangulation, proving it with a card model and marking it out on sheet.

blocks.note: Practise the geometry until it is quick: Pythagoras, tan and cos for roof pitches, true lengths, cone patterns and lobster-back segments. Many short answers are calculations, and the practicals need them before any steel is marked.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The biggest dangers in structural marking out are not the scriber and the punch, but the steel itself: beams and columns weighing hundreds or thousands of kilograms, which can fall, roll, tip or swing.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Lifting with a crane or hoist
A load swings, slips from its slings or drops; people are crushed.
Only trained people sling and signal
Lifting gear with a current inspection tag, used within its safe working load (SWL)
Tag lines to steady long loads
**Nobody stands or works under a suspended load**: lower it onto stands before anyone marks it
Turning a beam over
It falls or rolls without warning; hands and feet are trapped.
Plan the turn: crane with a beam clamp or turning sling, or a proper turning device
Never roll a heavy beam over with bars or let it drop onto the floor
Everyone clear before it moves
Stands and trestles
An overloaded or badly placed trestle collapses and drops the member.
Check each stand's SWL against the load it will carry, with a margin
Firm, level floor; stands spaced so the member is stable
Chock angles and channels so they cannot tip or roll
Long members
People walk into ends sticking out into walkways; members are knocked off their stands.
Flag or barrier the ends
Keep walkways clear; re-route people if needed
Pinch points
Fingers and hands trapped between steel and a stand or another member.
Keep hands off the steel while it moves
Use push sticks or tag lines, not hands
Sharp edges and points
Cuts from flame-cut edges; stab wounds from trammel and scriber points.
Gloves when handling
Points capped when not in use
Laser levels
Eye injury from looking into the beam.
Never look into the beam or point it at people
Follow the maker's class and safety label

flow: Plan the turn: weight, crane, clamp or sling, who signals, where people stand
Check the lifting gear's SWL and inspection tags
Clear the area and warn everyone nearby
Lift just clear, check the load is balanced and secure
Turn it under control with the crane and tag lines
Lower it onto stands, chock it, and release the gear only when it is stable
Only then start marking

blocks.note: Steel left in the sun in an open yard gets hot enough to burn, and the afternoon showers make it slippery. Stop crane lifts in strong wind and during thunderstorms, and bring work under cover where you can.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Structural sections, shop drawings and checking the steel

head: Section
Parts you mark from
rows: Universal beam (UB) and column (UC)

**Flanges** (top and bottom), **web** (the upright plate), **root radius** (the curved fillet where web meets flange), flange **toes** (the outer edges), flange **outstand** (from the web face to the toe)
Channel (PFC)
Web, two flanges, the **back** of the web, flange toes, root radius
Angle
Two legs, the **heel** (outside corner), the **toes** (ends of the legs), the root (inside corner)
Hollow sections (SHS, RHS, CHS)
Faces and corner radii; the weld seam of the tube

ul: The **general arrangement (GA)** or erection drawing shows the whole structure and where each **piece mark** (for example B12 or C3) goes.
Each piece mark has a **shop drawing** giving its section, length, holes, copes, cleats and welds. Mark each member from **its own shop drawing**, not from the GA.
Paint the piece mark on every member in the same place each time (for example near one end of the web), so the erectors can find it.

blocks.p: Marks squared from a bent or twisted member end up in the wrong place. Check every member **before** you mark it.

head: Check
What it is
How to check
rows: Section and grade
The size and grade the drawing asks for
Measure depth, width and thickness; check labels or mill certificates if the job needs them
Length
Enough for the part and its allowances
Tape from a squared end
**Sweep**
A sideways bow, seen when looking down on the member
String line with equal spacers at each end; measure the gap along the length
**Camber**
An upward (or downward) bow in the plane of the web
String line or level along the flange
Twist
The ends are turned relative to each other
Spirit level across the flange at each end on level stands, or sight across two straight edges
Flange out of square, damage
Flanges tilted, dents, nicks, laminations
Square against the web; look along the member

blocks.p: **String line method:** fix a string tight between two equal spacers (for example 25 mm blocks) at each end of the member. Anywhere the gap between string and steel is not 25 mm shows the bow at that point. The job specification gives the bow allowed; if a member is outside it, report it before marking.

ul: Use a good steel tape, and use the **same tape** for the whole job. Tapes from different makers can differ by a millimetre or more over 10 m: check each against the shop's reference tape.
**Support** the tape along its length and pull it to a steady tension; a sagging or slack tape reads long.
For an accurate reading, start from a clear graduation, for example the 100 mm line, held exactly on the datum, and subtract 100 mm, rather than trusting the hook.
Measure every size from the **datum** (an end, a centre line or a working point), not from mark to mark.
Keep tape and steel at the same temperature: do not measure steel in the sun with a tape kept in the shade.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Chalk line
Long straight lines on floors and plates
Trammels or a tape with a scriber
Large arcs, such as striking a truss apex
Laser level or water level
Carrying a level line round a large member or across a site
Plumb bob
Vertical lines
Sliding bevel with a protractor
Setting out and transferring angles, such as skew cuts
Large squares, flange squares and wrap-around bands
Square lines across flanges and round sections

blocks.note: If two members on a drawing would clash, or sizes do not add up, stop and send a query to the drawing office. Do not move holes or cut members shorter to 'make it fit'.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Marking members: datums, holes, gauge lines and back marks

ul: Use the datum the shop drawing uses: often one **end** of the member, the **centre line** of the web or flange, or a **working point** where centre lines meet.
If every hole is dimensioned from the beam's centre line, mark and check that centre line first.

To square a line round an I-section: square across the top flange from the web centre line, carry the line down the web with a square held against the flange, and across the bottom flange. Check that the lines meet at the edges.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Pitch
The distance between hole centres **along** a line of holes
Gauge
The distance of a line of holes from a reference line or edge, across the member
Cross-centres
On a beam flange, the distance **across** the flange between the two lines of holes, one each side of the web
Back mark
On an angle, the distance from the **heel** to the line of holes; on a channel, from the back of the web
End distance
From the centre of the end hole to the end of the member or plate
Edge distance
From a hole centre to the nearest edge, measured across
Staggered holes
Holes on one line placed midway between those on the other line

ul: Flange holes in a UB or UC are on **two gauge lines**, equal each side of the web, because the web is in the way at the centre and the bolts need room clear of the root radius and for the spanner.
On an **unequal angle**, each leg has its own back mark, because the legs are different widths.
With staggered holes at a pitch p on each line, the distance along the member from a hole on one line to the next hole on the other line is p ÷ 2.

**End and edge distances:** too small, and the bolt can tear out through the edge; too large, and the plates can gape and let in water. Codes set minimum values, often about 1.2 to 1.5 times the hole diameter; the drawing gives the sizes to use. Check every one.

flow: Check the member for sweep and twist on level stands
Mark the datum: a square end line or the centre line
Mark the gauge lines (or back marks) from the drawing, equal about the web centre line
Mark the end distance to the first hole, then each pitch, all measured from the datum
Check the edge distances
Light punch, check every size against the drawing, then punch fully and scribe guide circles
Paint the piece mark; a second person checks and signs

ul: **Splice plates and flanges:** mark both from one template, or clamp them together and drill them as a pair, so every hole lines up. Match-mark the pair.

**Base plates on anchor bolts already cast in concrete:** make a template from the bolts themselves (plywood or hardboard laid over them, with the holes, centre lines and the column's facing direction marked), and compare it with the base plate before drilling. Concrete work is rarely exact.
**Holes in a welded member that must line up with other steel:** often drilled after welding, or held by a drilling jig, because weld shrinkage moves parts.

blocks.p: When a member meets another at an angle in plan, its end is cut skew. If a beam meets a column face at 70°, the cut line is 90° − 70° = **20° from square**. Across a flange 146 mm wide, one corner is set back 146 × tan 20° = 146 × 0.364 = **53.1 mm** from the other. Set the angle on a sliding bevel with a protractor, mark it, and check the set-back with a rule.

blocks.note: Mark the waste side of every cut, the piece mark, and which holes are drilled and which are site-drilled. Clear marks save mistakes at the saw and the drill.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Copes, notches, stiffeners and weld preparations

blocks.p: A **cope** is a cut-away at the end of a beam, through part of the flange and web, so that it fits under or into the flange of the member that supports it, with the tops level.

ul: **Depth** of a top cope: the supporting member's flange thickness + its root radius + a small clearance (often a few millimetres). Example: a 12 mm flange with a 10 mm root radius and 5 mm clearance gives a cope 27 mm deep.

**Length** of the cope: the supporting member's flange outstand (about half its flange width less half its web) plus a clearance, measured from the end of the coped beam. The drawing usually gives both sizes.
The inside corner of a cope is always marked with a **radius** (often about 10 to 15 mm, or as drawn), never a sharp square corner. A sharp corner concentrates stress, and a crack can start there.

Mark a square line across the flange and down the web at the cope length, then the cope depth along the web, then the radius with dividers or a template. Show the waste clearly. After flame cutting, the edge is ground smooth.

To bend an angle round a corner, cut a **V-notch** out of one leg and bend the other leg. The notch angle equals the angle the member turns through: **90°** for a square corner, **60°** for each corner of a regular hexagon (where the inside angle is 120°).
Mark the bend line first, then the two sides of the V from the point where the bend line meets the other leg.
A mitred corner joining two pieces of angle or channel at 90° has each piece cut at 45°.

A full-depth **web stiffener** fits between the flanges at a point load or support. Its height is the clear depth between the flanges: beam depth − 2 × flange thickness. Its width is no more than the flange outstand, so it does not stick out past the flange toes.
Example: a beam 406 mm deep with 13 mm flanges has a clear depth of 406 − 26 = **380 mm**.
The two inside corners of each stiffener are cut off at an angle, called **snipes**, so the stiffener clears the root radius and the web-to-flange weld. The drawing gives their size.
A drawing note 'fit to bear' means the stiffener must sit tight against the flange: mark and cut it to fit closely.
Mark stiffener positions on the web from the datum, on both sides where the drawing shows pairs.

blocks.p: A **web penetration** is an opening cut in a beam web, often round, to let a pipe or duct pass through. Mark its centre from the datums, scribe the circle, and mark any reinforcing plate or ring the drawing shows. Never add an opening the drawing does not show: it weakens the beam.

The **welding procedure specification (WPS)** gives the bevel angle and root face. Mark the root face line on the plate edge and the bevel line on the face, so the cutter can produce exactly that preparation.

Distance of the bevel line from the edge, on the face = (plate thickness − root face) × tan(bevel angle). Example: 12 mm plate, 30° bevel, 2 mm root face: (12 − 2) × tan 30° = 10 × 0.577 = **5.8 mm**. Check the cut edge with a bevel gauge and a rule after cutting.

blocks.note: At Level 3 you read the WPS the Centre uses and check the preparation against it before fit-up. A wrong root face or angle gives lack of fusion or burn-through, whoever does the welding.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Setting out trusses, frames and stairs full size

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Span
The distance between the supports (eaves nodes), on the setting-out lines
Run
Half the span, for a symmetrical truss
Rise
The height of the apex above the eaves setting-out line
Pitch
The slope of the roof: as an angle (for example 20°), or as a ratio of rise to run (for example 1 in 4: 1 m up for every 4 m across)
Rafter length
The length of the top chord on its setting-out line, from the eaves node to the apex
Node (working point)
The point where the setting-out lines of members meet
Chords, struts and ties
Top and bottom members, and the inside members carrying compression and tension

blocks.note: Pitch is written in different ways. '1 in 4' usually means rise to run, but some older drawings give rise as a fraction of the whole span, so 'quarter pitch' can mean a rise of a quarter of the span, which is much steeper. Check how the drawing means it before you calculate.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Rafter length = √(run² + rise²). Span 9 m, rise 2 m: run 4.5 m, rafter = √(4.5² + 2²) = √24.25 = **4.924 m**.
Pitch angle = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ run). For the same truss: tan⁻¹(2 ÷ 4.5) = **24.0°**.
From an angle: rise = run × tan(pitch), and rafter = run ÷ cos(pitch). Span 7.2 m at 20°: rise = 3.6 × 0.364 = **1.310 m**; rafter = 3.6 ÷ 0.940 = **3.831 m**.

Inside members: work out the coordinates of each node from the eaves node, then each member length by Pythagoras. In the 9 m truss, a strut from the foot of the centre post to the middle of a rafter runs from (4.5, 0) to (2.25, 1.0): its length is √(2.25² + 1.0²) = 2.462 m.

blocks.h: Setting out a truss full size

flow: Clean the floor or plate table and check it is flat; the setting-out must be easy to see
Snap a straight base line for the bottom chord's setting-out line, and mark a centre line square to it (3-4-5 or intersecting arcs)
Mark the two eaves nodes at half the span either side of the centre line
From each eaves node, strike an arc of the rafter length with trammels or a tape; where the arcs cross on the centre line is the apex
Check the apex height against the rise
Draw the setting-out line of every member and mark every node
Check: span, rise, both halves equal (measure matching points from the centre line) and the diagonals
Draw the member outlines (for example the backs of the angles) from the setting-out lines
Lay each piece of steel on the layout to mark its cut lines and angles; make gusset templates from the layout
Fix stops or tack blocks so the layout can be used as an assembly jig; record the sizes

ul: If the two apex arcs cross off the centre line, the eaves nodes are not equally spaced about it, or the arcs were struck at different radii. Find and correct the error before marking any steel.

The drawing says which line of each member is set out to the node: the centre line, the back-mark (bolt) line or the centroid line. Use that line, or the members will not meet at the nodes as designed.
Gussets marked straight from the layout take their true shape and angles from it. Mark the member positions on each gusset.
Each **rise** = total rise ÷ number of risers. A floor-to-floor height of 2720 mm with 16 risers gives 170 mm risers.
Each **going** is the drawing's figure; with one fewer going than risers on a straight flight, 15 goings of 250 mm give a total going of 3750 mm.
Stringer angle = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ going) = tan⁻¹(170 ÷ 250) = 34.2°.
A common comfort check is twice the rise plus the going, which should be about 550 to 700 mm: 2 × 170 + 250 = 590 mm. Building rules and the drawing set the limits.
Mark the tread positions on both stringers from the **same datum** (the bottom), lay the two stringers side by side to compare them, and check the top against the landing before cutting.

blocks.note: Before you clean off a full-size layout, check that the whole batch has been marked, assembled and checked, and record the layout's key sizes (and photos) in case the job is repeated.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Allowances: weld shrinkage, camber, bending and rolling

blocks.p: Welds shrink as they cool and pull the parts with them. Long welds make a member shorter and can bow it; welds across a member pull it shorter at that joint. On heavily welded members such as built-up columns and plate girders:

ul: Add a shrinkage allowance to the marked length, taken from the shop's procedure or past jobs, or
Leave the ends long and trim them to length after welding, and
Mark holes that must line up with other steel after welding, not before.

blocks.p: **Camber** on a drawing means the member is to be made with an upward curve, highest at mid-span, so that it settles straight under its load or after welding. 'Camber 15 mm' means 15 mm up at mid-span.

ul: For a built-up girder, the web plate is marked and cut with curved top and bottom edges, and the flanges are fitted to the curve.

Set out a straight base line, mark stations along it, and at each station mark the camber offset. Where only the mid-span figure is given, a parabola is usual (check with the engineer): offset = C × (1 − (2x ÷ L)²), where C is the mid-span camber, L the length and x the distance from mid-span.
Example: L = 8 m, C = 12 mm, stations every metre: offsets 12 mm at mid-span, 11.25 mm at 1 m from it, 9 mm at 2 m, 5.25 mm at 3 m and 0 at the ends.
Check the camber again after welding with a string line at the stations, and record it.

blocks.p: When plate is bent, the outside **stretches** and the inside is **squeezed**. In between is a line that keeps its length: the **neutral axis**, about a third to a half of the thickness in from the inside of the bend. The flat blank is therefore shorter than the sum of the outside sizes.

Blank length = the straight (flat) lengths + a **bend allowance** for each bend. Bend allowance = (angle ÷ 360) × 2π × (inside radius + K × thickness), where K is about 0.33 to 0.5. Example: 8 mm plate bent to 90° with an 8 mm inside radius, outside legs 120 mm and 80 mm. Flats: 120 − 16 = 104 mm and 80 − 16 = 64 mm. With K = 0.4, bend allowance = 0.25 × 2 × 3.142 × (8 + 3.2) = 17.6 mm. Blank = 104 + 64 + 17.6 = **185.6 mm**, not 200 mm.

blocks.note: K depends on the material, the thickness, the radius and the press tooling. Bend a test piece from the same plate, measure it, and adjust before you mark the batch.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A plate rolled into a cylinder is developed on its **mean diameter** (the diameter at the middle of the thickness): mean diameter = inside diameter + thickness, or outside diameter − thickness.
Blank length = π × mean diameter. A shell 800 mm outside diameter from 8 mm plate: mean diameter 792 mm, blank 3.142 × 792 = **2488.5 mm**.
Add any allowance the shop uses for trimming the flat ends left by the rolls, and for the seam weld gap.
Saw kerf and flame-cut width between pieces cut from one bar or plate.
Machining allowance on edges or faces to be machined.
Lap and seam allowances on sheet-metal patterns (see Developments).

blocks.p: A **development** (or pattern) is the flat shape that, when cut and bent or rolled, makes the finished part. There are three methods.

head: Method
Used for
How it works
rows: Parallel line
Prisms and cylinders: pipe cut at an angle, pipe branches, mitred and lobster-back bends
Lines parallel to the axis are carried from the views onto a straight stretch-out line
Radial line
Right cones and pyramids, with the apex straight above the centre of the base: cone frustums, hoppers
All lines come from one point, the apex; the pattern is a sector of a circle
Triangulation
Everything else: oblique cones, square-to-round and offset transitions
The surface is split into triangles; the true length of every line is found and the triangles are rebuilt flat

blocks.p: A sloping line looks shorter in plan than it really is. Its **true length** is the long side of a right-angled triangle whose base is the plan length and whose upright is the vertical height between its ends: true length = √(plan length² + height²). Example: plan length 180 mm, height 240 mm: √(180² + 240²) = √90 000 = **300 mm**. On the drawing board, draw the triangle and measure its long side.

ul: The **slant height** L of a right cone = √(base radius² + vertical height²).
The pattern is a sector of a circle of radius L. Its angle = 360° × base radius ÷ L.
Example: base 500 mm diameter (radius 250), height 600 mm: L = √(250² + 600²) = 650 mm; sector angle = 360 × 250 ÷ 650 = **138.5°**.

A **frustum** is a cone with its top cut off parallel to the base. Work out the full cone, then the small cone that is cut off (by similar triangles), and draw two arcs from the same apex. If the cone above is cut at 250 mm diameter (half its base), the small cone's slant height is half as well, 325 mm, so the frustum pattern lies between arcs of 650 mm and 325 mm radius, over 138.5°.
For plate, use the mean diameters. Add lap or seam allowances along the joint edge, and an allowance for any flange or rolled edge.

flow: Draw the plan full size: the square and the circle in their true positions; and an elevation showing the height
Divide the circle into equal parts, usually 12, and number the points
Join each point to the nearest corner of the square, splitting the surface into flat triangles and curved corner sections
Find the true length of every line from its plan length and the height; write them in a true-length table
Choose the seam line (often at the middle of one flat side)
Build the pattern from the seam, one triangle at a time, using the true lengths and the true spaces (the chord between circle points and the sides of the square)
Join the circle points with a smooth curve and the square corners with straight lines; mark bend lines
Cut the pattern in card, bend it up, and check that it closes, the top is round and the base square, before marking steel

blocks.p: When the round top is centred over the square, each quarter of the transition is the same, so only a few different true lengths are needed. When it is offset, every line can be different and must be found separately.

ul: A **wrap-around template** is drawn on thin card, plastic or sheet and wrapped round the outside of the pipe to mark a cut. Its **stretch-out** is the pipe's outside circumference: OD × π. For 114.3 mm OD pipe: 114.3 × 3.142 = **359.1 mm**, divided into 12 parts of 29.9 mm.
When the pipe itself is to be made from sheet and rolled, use the **mean** diameter instead.
Mark the pipe's **quarter lines** and the matching lines on the template, line them up, wrap the template tightly, and scribe or soapstone round it.

blocks.p: For a 90° branch whose centre line meets the main's centre line, the branch end is developed by the **parallel line** method: divide the branch's end view into 12, project each line to where it meets the main pipe's outline, and carry those heights onto the 12 divisions of the stretch-out. Join the points with a smooth curve. A **set-on** branch sits on the outside of the main, which has a hole the size of the branch bore; a **set-in** branch passes into a hole the size of its outside diameter. The hole in the main is marked with its own template.

ul: A **lobster-back bend** is made of short mitred pieces of straight pipe welded together, with a half segment at each end and full segments between.
Number of joints (welds) = number of full segments + 1.
Each joint turns the pipe through (bend angle ÷ number of joints), and each cut face is **half of that** from square.
A full segment's length on the centre line = 2 × bend radius × tan(cut angle); a half segment's is half that, plus any straight length.

head: 90° bend
Turn at each joint
Each cut from square
rows: 2 joints (1 full + 2 half)
3 joints (2 full + 2 half)
4 joints (3 full + 2 half)

blocks.p: Example: a 3-joint 90° bend with a 300 mm bend radius in 168.3 mm OD pipe. Each cut is 15° from square, so a full segment is 2 × 300 × tan 15° = 600 × 0.268 = **160.8 mm** on the centre line, about 206 mm on the back (outside) and 116 mm on the throat (inside).

blocks.note: Lay out the bend full size on the floor: its centre-line radius, the joint lines and the two ends at 90°. Check the tacked segments against it before welding; small errors at each joint add up to a bend that is not square.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Checking, records and leading the team

flow: Check that you have the latest GA and shop drawings and that the revisions match
Make a list of every piece mark: section, length, holes, copes, stiffeners, cleats
Check the delivered steel against the list: section, grade, length, straightness, damage
Check the tools: tapes against the shop reference, squares against the master, levels
Plan the order: plates and small parts from templates; long members; full-size layouts
Share the work by skill; pair trainees with experienced markers
Brief the team: drawings, datums, checks, lifting plan and safety
First-off check of each piece type, then a second person checks every piece

ul: **First-off check:** the first piece of each type is fully checked against the drawing before the rest are marked.

**Second checker:** a second person checks every piece against the drawing and tolerances (for example ±2 mm on length), including diagonals, hole patterns, copes and stiffener positions, and signs the check sheet.

**Fit-up check:** parts that must fit together are checked together before cutting: splice plates against flanges, base plates against the anchor-bolt template, the two stringers of a stair side by side, a landing frame against the stringer tops.
A piece outside tolerance is re-marked before it is cut; the old marks are cancelled clearly.

head: The check sheet records
Why
rows: Piece mark, drawing number and revision
Ties the check to the right piece and drawing
Sizes checked, tolerance, result
Shows the piece was checked, and against what
The tape (or other tool) used
If a tape is later found faulty, every piece it measured can be traced
Marker's and checker's names, date
Responsibility and a record for quality checks
Faults found and what was done
So repeated faults can be traced to their cause

ul: Sizes do not add up, or members clash: stop and send a written query to the drawing office; record the answer on the drawing.
The same error keeps happening: the team leader finds the cause (a faulty tape, a misread drawing, a wrong datum) and fixes it, not only the pieces.
A piece is cut wrong: quarantine and label it, and report it; do not hide it in the batch.
Give each person clear tasks, the drawings they need and the checks expected.
Supervise lifting and turning yourself; nobody improvises a lift.
Check progress against the piece-mark list and keep it ticked off.
Teach trainees the reasons: why datums, why radii on copes, why a second checker.
At the end of the job, store and label marked pieces, file the check sheets, and record layout sizes before clearing the floor.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can plan the safe lifting, turning and support of heavy sections, and explain why nobody works under a suspended load.
I can name the parts of beams, channels and angles used in marking out.
I can explain how GA drawings, shop drawings and piece marks are used.
I can check a member for sweep, camber and twist, and measure long lengths accurately.
I can explain pitch, gauge, cross-centres, back mark, end and edge distance and staggered holes.
I can mark a hole group on a beam and make matching holes line up.
I can make a template from cast-in anchor bolts.
I can work out and mark a skew cut.
I can size and mark a cope with a radius, and explain why the radius matters.
I can work out the notch angle for bending an angle.
I can size a stiffener and explain its snipes.
I can mark a weld preparation from the WPS.
I can work out rafter lengths, rises, pitch angles and member lengths for a truss.
I can set out a truss full size, check it and use it to mark members and gussets.
I can work out stair rises and goings and mark matching stringers.
I can allow for weld shrinkage, camber, bending and rolling.
I can find a true length and develop patterns by parallel line, radial line and triangulation.
I can make a wrap-around template and work out lobster-back segment angles and lengths.
I can run first-off and second-person checks and keep a check sheet.
I can lead a marking team and deal with queries and errors correctly.

terms: Back mark
On an angle, the distance from the heel to the line of holes
Camber
An upward curve, highest at mid-span, made in a beam or girder on purpose
Cope
A cut-away at the end of a beam so it fits under or into another member
Cross-centres
The distance across a flange between the two lines of holes
Development
The flat pattern of a part before it is bent or rolled
Edge distance
The distance from a hole centre to the nearest edge
First-off check
A full check of the first piece before the rest of the batch
Frustum
A cone with its top cut off parallel to its base
Gauge line
A line of holes set a given distance from a reference line or edge
Lobster-back bend
A pipe bend made from short mitred pieces of straight pipe
Mean diameter
The diameter measured to the middle of the plate thickness
Neutral axis
The line in a bent plate that keeps its length
Node (working point)
The point where the setting-out lines of members meet
Parallel line development
A method for prisms and cylinders using lines parallel to the axis
Piece mark
The code painted on a member to show where it goes
Pitch
The distance between hole centres along a line
Radial line development
A method for right cones and pyramids using lines from the apex
Rise
The height of a roof apex above the eaves, or of one stair step
Root radius
The curved fillet where a beam's web meets its flange
Snipe
A small corner cut-off on a stiffener to clear the root radius and welds
Span
The distance between the supports of a truss or beam
Stretch-out
A straight line equal to the circumference, on which a pipe pattern is drawn
Sweep
A sideways bow in a member, seen when looking down on it
Triangulation
A development method that splits a surface into triangles of true length
True length
The real length of a sloping line, found from its plan length and height
Web penetration
An opening cut in a beam web for a pipe or duct
Wrap-around template
A flexible pattern wrapped round a pipe to mark a cut

c1.title: Roof trusses in Lucea
c1.text: Mikhail leads the team setting out angle roof trusses for a community centre in Lucea, Hanover. Each truss has a span of 10.8 m and a rise of 1.8 m on its setting-out lines, with a centre post and a strut from the foot of the centre post to the middle of each rafter. The team will set out one truss full size on the plate table and use it to mark the members and gussets for six trusses.

c2.title: Mezzanine beams in May Pen
c2.text: Patrice's team is marking universal beams for a warehouse mezzanine in May Pen, Clarendon. The secondary beams are coped to sit with their tops level with the main beams, whose flanges are 12 mm thick with a 10 mm root radius; the drawing asks for 5 mm clearance. Some secondary beams meet the main beams at an angle in plan. The main beams are 406 mm deep with 13 mm flanges and need full-depth stiffeners. Two markers measuring the same 7.2 m between hole groups get 7203 mm and 7198 mm.

c3.title: A feed hopper in Hayes
c3.text: Rojae is developing a hopper for a poultry farm in Hayes, Clarendon. It is a cone frustum with its large end at the top: 900 mm diameter at the top, 300 mm diameter at the outlet, and 400 mm high, with the outlet centred under the top. It will be made from 3 mm sheet in one piece, joined by a lapped and welded seam.

c4.title: A lobster-back bend near Black River
c4.text: Delroy is setting out a 90° lobster-back bend for an irrigation pump station near Black River, St Elizabeth. The bend is made from 168.3 mm outside diameter pipe with three joints, so each cut face is 15° from square, and the bend radius on the centre line is 300 mm.

c5.title: A long beam in an Ewarton yard
c5.text: Shavar's team must mark both flanges of a 9 m beam weighing about 1100 kg in a fabrication yard in Ewarton, St Catherine. A trainee has set it on two trestles, each with a rating plate reading 'SWL 500 kg'. One end of the beam sticks out about 1.5 m into the walkway to the stores.

questions.q: What is the pitch angle of Mikhail's trusses?
questions.why: Pitch angle = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ run) = tan⁻¹(1.8 ÷ 5.4) = 18.4°. Using the whole span (tan⁻¹(1.8 ÷ 10.8) = 9.5°) or turning the ratio upside down (71.6°) are common slips.

questions.q: How long is each strut, from the foot of the centre post to the middle of a rafter, on its setting-out line?
questions.why: Taking the eaves node as (0, 0), the foot of the centre post is at (5.4, 0) and the middle of the rafter at (2.7, 0.9). The strut is √(2.7² + 0.9²) = √8.1 = 2.85 m.

questions.q: On the plate table, the two arcs struck for the apex cross 15 mm to one side of the centre line. What does this show?
o: The rise on the drawing is wrong, so the apex can stay where it is
The plate table is not level, so it must be packed before going on
The truss must be built off centre, as the arcs have shown
The eaves node marks or the two arc radii are unequal
questions.why: Two equal arcs from eaves nodes placed equally either side of the centre line must cross on it. The span marks and the arc radius are checked and corrected before any steel is marked.

questions.q: Which line of each angle should the team set out to the nodes?
o: Always the heel of each angle, since it is the easiest to see
The line the drawing gives, such as the back-mark line
Always the toe of each angle, so the legs meet at the nodes
Whichever line lets each member be cut to the shortest length
questions.why: The designer decides how the members meet at each node, and the drawing says which line is used. Using a different line moves the members off the nodes and changes how the truss carries load.

questions.q: How deep should the top cope on the secondary beams be?
questions.why: Cope depth = the main beam's flange thickness + its root radius + clearance = 12 + 10 + 5 = 27 mm. Leaving out the root radius (17 mm) makes the cope foul the fillet.

questions.q: One secondary beam's end is cut 20° from square across its 146 mm flange. How far is one corner of the cut set back from the other? (tan 20° = 0.364)
questions.why: The set-back is the flange width × tan(skew angle): 146 × 0.364 = 53.1 mm. Mark it with a sliding bevel set to 20° and check the set-back with a rule.

questions.q: What is the height of each full-depth stiffener for the main beams, before the snipes are cut?
questions.why: A full-depth stiffener fits between the flanges: 406 − (2 × 13) = 380 mm. The snipes at its inside corners clear the root radius and welds; they do not change its height.

questions.q: What should Patrice do about the two different 7.2 m measurements?
o: Take the average, 7200.5 mm, and mark the holes from that figure
Use the longer reading, as a longer beam can always be cut back
Check both tapes against the shop's reference tape, then re-measure
Use the shorter reading, since the hook of a tape always adds length
questions.why: A 5 mm difference over 7.2 m points to a faulty tape or poor technique. Checking both tapes against the reference, then re-measuring from the same datum with the tape supported and pulled steadily, finds the true size.

questions.q: What radius is the large arc of Rojae's pattern?
questions.why: The full cone has a base radius of 450 mm and, by similar triangles, a height of 600 mm, so its slant height is √(450² + 600²) = 750 mm. 500 mm is the slant length of the frustum alone.

questions.q: What angle does the sector of Rojae's pattern cover?
questions.why: Sector angle = 360° × base radius ÷ slant height = 360 × 450 ÷ 750 = 216°. The 144° left over is the part of the circle that is not used.

questions.q: What must Rojae add to the pattern because of the lapped seam?
o: A lap allowance along one of the straight joint edges
An extra 216° sector so that the hopper has two layers
Nothing, since a lapped seam is welded and needs no extra
A lap allowance round both the top and outlet curves
questions.why: A lap joint needs the two straight edges to overlap, so extra metal is added along one of them. Allowances on the curved edges are only needed for flanges or rolled edges.

questions.q: How long is one full segment of Delroy's bend, measured on its centre line? (tan 15° = 0.268)
questions.why: A full segment has a 15° cut at each end, so its centre-line length is 2 × bend radius × tan 15° = 2 × 300 × 0.268 = 160.8 mm. 80.4 mm is a half segment.

questions.q: Before welding, how should Delroy check the tacked bend?
o: Measure one segment carefully and assume the other segments match
Weld it fully first, then check it against the pipe it will join
Lay it on a full-size set-out and check the ends are at 90°
Check by eye that every cut face looks square to the pipe
questions.why: Small errors at each joint add up round the bend. A full-size set-out shows the centre-line radius and the two ends at 90°, so the bend can be corrected before the joints are welded.

questions.q: What should Shavar do about the trestles?
o: Use them, since between them they are rated for 1000 kg
Use them, but tell the team not to lean on the beam
Put timber packing on top of them to spread the load
Use stands rated for the load, with a margin to spare
questions.why: Each trestle carries about half of 1100 kg, more than its 500 kg rating, and the load is never shared exactly. Overloaded stands can collapse and drop the beam.

questions.q: How should the end sticking into the walkway be dealt with?
o: Leave it, as anyone can see a beam of that size in the way
Barrier or flag it, and keep people away from that end
Ask people to step over it carefully whenever they pass
Tie a rag on it, and move the beam when the job is done
questions.why: People walk into or trip over ends that stick out, and a knock can move the beam on its stands. A barrier or clear flag, and a clear route round, keep people away.

questions.q: A line in a transition has a plan length of 200 mm and a vertical height of 400 mm. What is its true length?
questions.why: True length = √(plan length² + height²) = √(200² + 400²) = √200 000 = 447.2 mm. Adding the two (600 mm) or subtracting squares (346.4 mm) are common slips.

questions.q: A 10 m beam is to have a camber of 20 mm at mid-span, set out as a parabola. What is the camber offset 2.5 m in from each end?
questions.why: 2.5 m from the end is 2.5 m from mid-span, so offset = 20 × (1 − (2 × 2.5 ÷ 10)²) = 20 × (1 − 0.25) = 15 mm. A parabola is flatter near the middle than a straight-line taper.

questions.q: A 12 mm plate needs a 30° bevel with a 2 mm root face. How far from the edge, on the plate face, is the bevel line? (tan 30° = 0.577)
questions.why: Only the 10 mm above the root face is bevelled, so the line is (12 − 2) × tan 30° = 5.8 mm in from the edge. Using the full 12 mm gives 6.9 mm, which would leave no root face.

questions.q: A staircase has a floor-to-floor height of 2975 mm and 17 risers. What is the height of each rise?
questions.why: Each rise = total rise ÷ number of risers = 2975 ÷ 17 = 175 mm. Every rise must be the same, so both stringers are marked from the same datum at the bottom.

questions.q: A frame in the shape of a regular hexagon is made by notching and bending one length of angle. What angle is each V-notch?
questions.why: At each corner of a regular hexagon the angle turns through 60° (its inside angle is 120°), and the V-notch equals the angle turned through.
